verses.text: Now the men of Israel had sworn in Mizpah, saying, “None of us will give his daughter to Benjamin as a wife.”
The people came to Bethel, and sat there until evening before God, and lifted up their voices, and wept severely.
They said, “Yahweh, the God of Israel, why has this happened in Israel, that there should be one tribe lacking in Israel today?”
On the next day, the people rose early, and built an altar there, and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings.

The children of Israel said, “Who is there among all the tribes of Israel who didn’t come up in the assembly to Yahweh?” For they had made a great oath concerning him who didn’t come up to Yahweh to Mizpah, saying, “He shall surely be put to death.”
The children of Israel grieved for Benjamin their brother, and said, “There is one tribe cut off from Israel today.
How shall we provide wives for those who remain, since we have sworn by Yahweh that we will not give them of our daughters to wives?”
They said, “What one is there of the tribes of Israel who didn’t come up to Yahweh to Mizpah?” Behold, no one came from Jabesh Gilead to the camp to the assembly.
For when the people were counted, behold, there were none of the inhabitants of Jabesh Gilead there.

The congregation sent twelve thousand of the most valiant men there, and commanded them, saying, “Go and strike the inhabitants of Jabesh Gilead with the edge of the sword, with the women and the little ones.
This is the thing that you shall do: you shall utterly destroy every male, and every woman who has lain with a man.”
They found among the inhabitants of Jabesh Gilead four hundred young virgins, who had not known man by lying with him; and they brought them to the camp to Shiloh, which is in the land of Canaan.
The whole congregation sent and spoke to the children of Benjamin who were in the rock of Rimmon, and proclaimed peace to them.
Benjamin returned at that time; and they gave them the women whom they had saved alive of the women of Jabesh Gilead. There still weren’t enough for them.
The people grieved for Benjamin, because Yahweh had made a breach in the tribes of Israel.
Then the elders of the congregation said, “How shall we provide wives for those who remain, since the women are destroyed out of Benjamin?”
They said, “There must be an inheritance for those who are escaped of Benjamin, that a tribe not be blotted out from Israel.
However we may not give them wives of our daughters, for the children of Israel had sworn, saying, ‘Cursed is he who gives a wife to Benjamin.’”

They said, “Behold, there is a feast of Yahweh from year to year in Shiloh, which is on the north of Bethel, on the east side of the highway that goes up from Bethel to Shechem, and on the south of Lebonah.”
They commanded the children of Benjamin, saying, “Go and lie in wait in the vineyards,

and see, and behold, if the daughters of Shiloh come out to dance in the dances, then come out of the vineyards, and each man catch his wife of the daughters of Shiloh, and go to the land of Benjamin.

It shall be, when their fathers or their brothers come to complain to us, that we will say to them, ‘Grant them graciously to us, because we didn’t take for each man his wife in battle, neither did you give them to them, otherwise you would now be guilty.’”

The children of Benjamin did so, and took wives for themselves, according to their number, of those who danced, whom they carried off. They went and returned to their inheritance, built the cities, and lived in them.
The children of Israel departed from there at that time, every man to his tribe and to his family, and they each went out from there to his own inheritance.
In those days there was no king in Israel. Everyone did that which was right in his own eyes.

footnotes.content: The men swore in Mizpah that no daughter should go to Benjamin—a binding oath meant to punish an unfathomable crime. But I've learned that swift judgments made in grief often bind us to paths we cannot undo. The oath was righteous anger; it just hadn't asked what would come after.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They came to Bethel and wept—the very place where God had been among them before, where Jacob had renamed the place "House of God." Now the whole people weeps, and their tears tell the Lord something no explanation could: we have broken ourselves. Even broken things come to Bethel seeking Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They ask why a tribe has gone missing from Israel—as if the horror itself could not have been prevented. The question shows they still don't see their own oath, their own hand in the loss. So often we ask God "why?" when we already know the answer, and shame keeps us from naming it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: On the next day they rose early and built an altar, offering burnt offerings and peace offerings—the mechanics of repentance, done right but coming too late. I notice the Lord does not thunder refusal, as He had in earlier days. He waits to see what His people will do when they are finally quiet enough to listen.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They ask who did not come to Mizpah and recall the great oath: "He shall surely be put to death." Jabesh Gilead will pay with its own blood for choosing not to witness their judgment. How quickly justice becomes a hunter of the innocent when we mistake our anger for God's will.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They grieve for Benjamin as a brother now—one tribe cut off from the rest. Grief comes now, too late to stop the harm. Yet I see something tender here: even after everything, they do not say "let him be gone." They cannot bear to lose him entirely, even though it was their own hands that struck.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "How shall we provide wives?" they ask, still bound by the oath. This is the voice of people trapped by their own word, seeking a loophole instead of breaking a promise. Sometimes wisdom is knowing when a vow was wrong and naming that before God—not hunting for clever ways around it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jabesh Gilead did not come to Mizpah—this becomes their condemnation. A town that missed one assembly will lose all its daughters. There is something terrifyingly final about the way one choice, one absence, can mark a place for destruction. It reminds me that history hangs on such thin threads.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When the people were counted, no one from Jabesh Gilead was there—and this absence is now evidence against them. They cannot explain, cannot defend themselves. They simply were not present at the gathering, and for that, their whole city will pay with blood and daughters taken.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Twelve thousand chosen warriors are sent to destroy everyone in Jabesh Gilead—men, women, children. I see the machinery of justice without mercy, ordered and systematic. And yet even in this darkness, there is a purpose hidden in the command: the young virgins will be spared. God's hand is not absent, though it is hidden.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Every male, every woman who has lain with a man—only the virgins remain alive. The command is brutal and specific, leaving no room for mercy or exception. And yet I see in this terrible specificity the only mercy that can exist in this moment: the preservation of innocence that will become redemption.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Four hundred young virgins are found and brought to Shiloh, the holy place where the tabernacle stands. What a strange mercy—to save these daughters from death, only to bring them into a scheme of capture and marriage. Yet their lives continue, and in God's economy, even this becomes a way forward.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They proclaim peace to Benjamin hiding in the rock of Rimmon—a peace offered to those who had become invisible, to men without a future. After the silence and shame, words are sent: "Come back. There is a way forward." Sometimes redemption begins with an unexpected offer of peace.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Benjamin comes out and receives the women, yet there still are not enough. Even with four hundred young women from Jabesh Gilead, the tribe's wound remains incomplete. It tells me that some losses cannot be fully restored—only honored by moving forward anyway.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The people grieve for Benjamin because the Lord had made a breach in the tribes of Israel. They finally see that the fracture came not from Benjamin alone, but from the Lord allowing their own judgment to run its course. Sometimes we must watch the full consequence of our words before we understand His hand in it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The elders ask again how to provide wives, now that the women of Benjamin are gone. They are still thinking in terms of solution-finding, still trying to close the gap with human cleverness. Yet notice the Lord has not stopped them—He is waiting to see what desperation might teach them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "There must be an inheritance for those who are escaped of Benjamin, that a tribe not be blotted out." Survival becomes the goal now, not perfection or honor. There is humility in this shift—no longer asking for justice to be pristine, only asking that one tribe continue to exist.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They cannot break the oath—"Cursed is he who gives a wife to Benjamin." So they do not give them wives. Instead, they will help them take them. Is this honoring an oath or discovering a loophole? I think it is both, and it shows how desperate people find ways to survive when bound by their own words.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: There is a feast of the Lord each year in Shiloh—a gathering, a holy place, daughters of Shiloh who will dance. The elders know the calendar of grace, the rhythm of worship. They will use the Lord's own feast as the place of their scheme. I've noticed how easily our plans attach themselves to sacred things when we stop asking permission.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Go and lie in wait in the vineyards—the command begins. They will hide among the fruit, among the growth, and watch. There is something deeply sorrowful about warriors forced to hide and ambush at a feast, at a time meant for joy and worship. Desperation makes us into creatures we never meant to be.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When the daughters of Shiloh dance in the dances, come out and catch your wife—each man for himself. They are reducing a woman to a prize to be caught, yet I notice the Lord allows this strange capture to become the instrument of a tribe's survival. His purposes are not our purposes, and sometimes redemption looks closer to rescue.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When the fathers and brothers come to complain, tell them: "We didn't take them in battle, and you didn't give them to us." It is the most transparent justification—almost an admission that they know what they are doing sounds like theft, like violation. Yet they ask the fathers to accept it, and somehow, they do.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Benjamin did so, and took wives according to their number, and returned to their inheritance to rebuild their cities. Life continues. A tribe that nearly died now lives again, built on a scheme that was part desperation, part mercy, part disobedience. The story does not resolve into cleanness, but into continuance.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Each man departed to his tribe and his family, each to his own inheritance. They scattered from Shiloh back to their homes, each carrying the weight of what had been done—the blood of Jabesh Gilead, the captured women, the broken oaths. The burden is shared now, dispersed across all tribes.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In those days there was no king in Israel, and everyone did that which was right in his own eyes. Readers today hear an echo here of our own times—not a prophecy, but a mirror. We too choose our own righteousness over God's word, bind ourselves with our own oaths, then scheme our way free. Looking back from 2026, I see how little has changed: we still need a King.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
